False.

The chapter, while explaining political leadership as a factor influencing foreign policy, states that 'Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru contributed the policy of non-alignment to India's foreign policy.' In the very next sentence it credits someone else with China: 'Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee contributed a great deal to improving Sino-Indian relations.' The chapter's own box on the contribution of Pandit Nehru lists only two things — his stand that India should independently understand global or international affairs, and his policy of peace.

About Nehru's period the chapter in fact says the opposite of friendship with China: 'The threats from China and Pakistan were also taken into account', and it lists conflict with China as one of the challenges of the first stage (1947-1990). The chapter places the start of the effort to mend relations with China much later — 'India initiated a dialogue to improve relations with China' from 1980, that is, after Nehru's time.

[Note: outside this chapter Pandit Nehru is often associated with early friendship efforts with China. But this chapter itself credits Atal Bihari Vajpayee, not Nehru, with improving Sino-Indian relations, so on the chapter's own evidence the statement is false.]

False.

The chapter says that 'Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee contributed a great deal to improving Sino-Indian relations' — that is, relations with China, not with Pakistan. Nowhere does the chapter say that Vajpayee took the lead in improving relations with Pakistan.

The only leader the chapter connects with Pakistan is Lal Bahadur Shastri, given as the worked example in the 'Complete the list' activity — 'Lal Bahadur Shastri : Tashkent Agreement'. For the rest, the chapter records India-Pakistan conflict rather than friendship: wars over the Kashmir question in 1947-48 and 1965, the war of 1971 in which Pakistan broke apart and Bangladesh was created, and 'conflict with Pakistan' listed among the challenges of the first stage.

[Note: outside this chapter Vajpayee is well known for steps towards Pakistan such as the bus journey to Lahore. But this chapter attributes to him the improvement of relations with China, so on the chapter's own evidence the statement is false.]

Foreign policy is the theoretical framework within which a country decides which nations it should be friendly with, which bloc it should participate in, and what position it should take in international relations. India got independence in 1947 and from then onwards began shaping its foreign policy independently. Its broad framework comes from Article 51 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, according to which India should give priority to safeguarding international peace and security, resolve international problems and disputes by peaceful means, maintain friendly relations with other nations and respect international law. India's foreign policy is based on values like international peace, human rights and security, and because conditions and national interest keep changing, it is always dynamic.

National interest implies the means through which the independence and sovereignty of our country can be safeguarded. It also includes efforts to achieve our economic development and to take steps towards increasing our national power. Defence, that is the protection of the country's independence, sovereignty and integrity, is the highest national interest; economic development comes next, because an economically weak nation will not be able to maintain its independence. National interest is considered to be the goal and foreign policy is considered to be the means to achieve it, and as conditions and times change, national interest also changes.

World peace means a condition in which nations live without war or conflict and settle their disputes by peaceful means instead of force. The chapter shows that peace has always been a central feature of India's foreign policy: Article 51 of the Constitution asks India to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration. Peace and freedom also became the fundamental principles of the policy of non-alignment. Because nuclear weapons are extremely destructive, the chapter says consistent efforts are necessary so that they are never used, and India has been consistently supporting efforts for disarmament, since it is India's position that there should be peace and security in the world.

[Note: the chapter does not give a formal, one-line definition of 'world peace'; the opening sentence above states the idea in the sense in which the chapter uses it, and everything after it is taken from the chapter.]

In my opinion, nuclear preparedness does threaten world peace, and the chapter supports this view. It states plainly that nuclear weapons are extremely destructive and that it is therefore necessary to make consistent efforts so that they are never used. It also points out that the number of countries making nuclear weapons is growing, so the danger keeps increasing. Two treaties, the Nuclear Non Proliferation Treaty (NNPT) and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT), were made to stop the spread of nuclear weapons; but their conditions benefit the big nuclear powers and put unfair restrictions on developing countries, and hence India has not signed either of them. India's own stand is that there should be peace and security in the world, and so India has been consistently supporting efforts for disarmament.

This is one defensible opinion, and a student may argue it differently. The other side can also be built from this chapter: India undertook the nuclear energy programme soon after independence mainly for electricity generation but also to create military capability, conducted nuclear tests in 1974 and 1998, and today has nuclear weapons and missiles that can carry them. From that point of view, nuclear capability is a part of a country's defence, which is its highest national interest. The chapter's own balance between the two views is that India has 'accepted the role of a responsible nuclear power' — it keeps its capability, but works for disarmament and peace at the same time.

India's foreign policy is based on values like international peace, human rights and security. Its broad framework is laid down by Article 51 of the Directive Principles of State Policy, which says India should promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised people with one another, and encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration. Following this, India gives priority to safeguarding international peace and security and to resolving international problems and disputes by peaceful means, while maintaining friendly relations with other nations. In the early period India's policy also rested on opposition to colonialism, an independent understanding of world events without pressure from any power, and insistence on self-reliance. Non-alignment, whose fundamental principles are peace and freedom, was adopted in the context of the cold war and remains an important principle of India's foreign policy.

Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee has contributed to improving Sino-Indian relations. While explaining political leadership as a factor that influences foreign policy, the chapter says that persons holding high positions try to maintain continuity in foreign policy and to improve upon it, and gives two examples — Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru contributed the policy of non-alignment to India's foreign policy, and 'Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee contributed a great deal to improving Sino-Indian relations.' The chapter also notes that from 1980 India initiated a dialogue to improve relations with China.

India's foreign policy is shaped within the framework of Article 51 of the Directive Principles of State Policy. Its objectives are:

1. To promote international peace and security, and to give priority to safeguarding it.
2. To maintain just, friendly and honourable relations between nations, and to resolve international problems and disputes by peaceful means.
3. To foster respect for international law and treaty obligations in the dealings of organised people with one another.
4. To encourage the settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
5. To keep friendly relations with neighbouring countries while ensuring that the defence and security of India is not affected, and not to compromise about the geographical boundaries of the nation.
6. To protect the unity and integrity of the country.
7. To protect the interests of India's citizens living in other countries, a responsibility fulfilled by the Indian embassies there.
8. To establish economic and commercial relations with other countries for achieving the economic development of India.

Concept map: the central box is 'Factors affecting Foreign Policy' and the five boxes around it are filled as follows.

1. Geographical Location - the size, population, topography, coastline, availability of natural resources and the position of a country in relation to its neighbours all have to be considered while deciding foreign policy.

2. Political System - in a democracy the parliament plays a major role in evolving foreign policy, the opposition parties regulate it by raising questions, and in a federal system the inclinations of the constituent States must be taken into account.

3. Economy - foreign policy is shaped by the need for trade, import-export and economic relations with other countries, and a country with a strong economy is less dependent on others and can have an independent foreign policy.

4. Political Leadership - the President, the Prime Minister, the Foreign Minister, the Defence Minister, the Finance Minister and the Home Minister decide foreign policy and try to maintain its continuity and improve upon it, as Pandit Nehru did with non-alignment and Atal Bihari Vajpayee did with Sino-Indian relations.

5. Administrative Factors - the Ministry of External Affairs, the Foreign Secretary, the embassies in different countries, diplomatic officers and the National Security Advisor collect and analyse the information needed to shape foreign policy and give appropriate advice.

| Factor | In one line |
|---|---|
| Geographical Location | Size, population, topography, coastline and natural resources shape the policy. |
| Political System | Parliament, opposition parties and constituent States influence the policy. |
| Economy | Trade needs and economic security decide how independent the policy can be. |
| Political Leadership | The Prime Minister and other key ministers give the policy its direction and continuity. |
| Administrative Factors | Ministry of External Affairs, embassies and diplomats gather information and advise. |
